identity.title: P-GenRM: Personalized Generative Reward Model with Test-time User-based Scaling

problem.claim: Personalized alignment needs accurate user-specific reward signals for open-ended scenarios.

gap.claim: Existing personalized reward models oversimplify scenario-specific preferences and generalize poorly to new users with limited feedback.

contributions.claim: P-GenRM converts preference signals into structured evaluation chains that derive adaptive personas and scoring rubrics across scenarios.
It combines individual-level adaptive scaling and aggregation with prototype-level transfer from similar users.
It introduces test-time user-based scaling for personalized generative reward modeling.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe P-GenRM as the first personalized generative reward model with test-time user-based scaling.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report state-of-the-art results on widely used personalized reward-model benchmarks, with an average improvement of approximately 2.31%.
The authors report strong generalization on an out-of-distribution dataset.
The authors report that test-time user-based scaling adds approximately a 3% boost.

narrative_sequence.summary: Personalized alignment adapts language-model responses to individual preferences, but open-ended settings require accurate user-specific rewards.
Existing reward models use overly small fixed principle sets and struggle with new users who provide little feedback.
P-GenRM builds structured evaluation chains, adaptive personas, scoring rubrics, User Prototypes, and dual-granularity scaling.
The authors report benchmark gains, out-of-distribution generalization, and an additional boost from test-time scaling.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links distinct failure modes to distinct design components: adaptive scenario rubrics address preference diversity, while prototype-level transfer addresses limited-feedback generalization.

lessons.interpretation: A compact abstract can make a method rationale legible by mapping each identified limitation to a corresponding mechanism.
lessons.application: When presenting a multi-component method, explicitly state which component targets each named limitation and preserve the mechanism-to-claim mapping.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when components interact inseparably or when the abstract lacks evidence isolating their roles.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the benchmarks, baseline methods, dataset sizes, evaluation protocol, or statistical uncertainty behind the reported improvements.
The out-of-distribution dataset and the conditions defining the approximately 3% test-time boost are unspecified.
The abstract does not report ablations that would isolate the effects of adaptive rubrics, user prototypes, and the two scaling granularities.
